steps.title: Chemical cell
steps.body: A device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy. It contains two different metals (electrodes) in an electrolyte. A voltage is produced because one metal is more reactive than the other.

steps.title: Fuel cell
steps.body: A cell that produces electrical energy from a fuel (e.g. hydrogen) and an oxidant (e.g. oxygen), as long as they are supplied. Unlike chemical cells, fuel cells do not run down or need recharging.

steps.title: Voltage
steps.body: The potential difference produced by a cell. The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage produced.

steps.title: How a chemical cell works
steps.body: The more reactive metal becomes the negative electrode because it more readily gives up electrons. These electrons flow through the external circuit to the less reactive metal. The further apart the two metals are in the reactivity series, the greater the voltage.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Type Features Examples Primary (non-rechargeable) Chemicals are used up; cannot be recharged Zinc-carbon, alkaline batteries Secondary (rechargeable) Can be recharged by reversing the reaction Lithium-ion, lead-acid car batteries

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Foundation Explain why a chemical cell needs two different metals and an electrolyte. | Foundation Which would produce the larger voltage — a cell using iron and copper, or a cell using magnesium and copper? Explain your answer. | Higher Write the half-equations and overall equation for a hydrogen fuel cell.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Two different metals are needed so one is more reactive than the other, creating a voltage (electrons flow from the more reactive metal). The electrolyte allows ions to move between the electrodes, co | Magnesium and copper produces the larger voltage. Magnesium is further from copper in the reactivity series than iron is. The greater the difference in reactivity, the greater the voltage. | Anode: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Cathode: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: For voltage questions: the further apart two metals are in the reactivity series, the greater the voltage Learn the hydrogen fuel cell half-equations — they are commonly tested In the fuel cell: oxidation happens at the anode (hydrogen loses electrons), reduction at the cathode (oxygen gains electrons) When discussing advantages/disadvantages of fuel cells, give balanced arguments Remember that although hydrogen fuel cells are clean, the hydrogen itself may not be — if produced from fossil fuels, there are still environmental issues Do not confuse chemical cells (which run down) with fuel cells (which keep going as long as fuel is supplied)
